content: 1. Support and training agencies should focus on areas of national or regional interest, ensuring transparency and open competition to identify the best projects based on scientific merit, potential impact, sustainability, integration of regional research capacity, and leveraging external funding to enhance national and regional research and training efforts. 2. Greater collaboration among nations facing similar health challenges and infectious diseases is essential to facilitate the exchange of experiences and training, which can contribute to achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). 3. Significant investment from both international and national funding bodies is required to develop facilities and enhance the capabilities of scientists who can lead research aimed at creating more effective tools and strategies to combat infectious diseases associated with poverty. 4. Improving prevention and control strategies for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) will contribute to poverty alleviation and the achievement of the MDGs. However, this requires strong commitment, political will, and transparent mechanisms to use health research as a driver for sustainable human resource development, economic growth, and poverty reduction. 5. Collaborative research is a highly effective means of strengthening research capacity. Scientists in disease-endemic countries often welcome partnerships with industrialized nations to overcome barriers to conducting research, obtaining training and funding, and exchanging ideas. 6. Unfortunately, scientists in disease-endemic countries are less enthusiastic about collaborating with neighboring countries within their own regions, partly due to limited funding opportunities for South-South collaborations. 7. Most health research and NTD capacity-building efforts in disease-endemic countries have been driven by institutions based in industrialized nations, rather than local initiatives. 8. The Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR) of the World Health Organization (WHO) has played a significant role in building research capacity over the past 30 years by sponsoring graduate training, providing re-entry grants for researchers to return to their home countries, and fostering South-South collaborations. 9. In 2010, TDR facilitated research and training exchanges between African scientists and the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, resulting in productive South-South connections between previously separate networks focused on schistosomiasis control. 10. The proposed relocation of the TDR-supported Initiative to Strengthen Health Research Capacity in Africa (ISHReCA) to Africa is a positive step, as it aims to enhance local research capacity with support from funders like the Wellcome Trust. 11. Other capacity-building initiatives, such as those by the African Capacity Building Foundation (ACBF) and partnerships with organizations like TWAS, aim to develop sustainable human and institutional capacity for poverty reduction in Africa. 12. Brazil has also contributed to South-South cooperation in health by training African students at postgraduate levels and establishing initiatives like the master's program in health sciences in Mozambique to support local health research and innovation. 13. Despite these efforts, research on NTDs and helminthiases in disease-endemic countries is often not prioritized, receiving minimal attention and funding due to limited national investments in research and competing priorities. 14. The outflow of trained staff from Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia is a significant challenge, driven by low salaries, poor working conditions, and a lack of institutional incentives to retain talent. 15. Building sustainable research capacity requires a comprehensive approach to human resource management and the development of a strong research culture in disease-endemic countries. 16. Governmental support for health research in disease-endemic countries is often insufficient, with low national investments and fragmented capacity-building efforts that fail to address the specific needs of different sectors. 17. Research capacity development is essential to generate evidence-based knowledge relevant to local health concerns and to inform policymakers in implementing effective practices. 18. There is a shortage of expertise in specialized areas critical for successful control measures, such as transmission dynamics modeling, advanced statistical analysis, parasite genetics, and monitoring resistance to antiparasitic drugs. 19. Mentorship programs are crucial for fostering the next generation of scientists in disease-endemic countries, providing guidance, research facilities, and networking opportunities to support career development. 20. The introduction of junior fellowships by initiatives like the European Foundation Initiative for African Research into Neglected Tropical Diseases (EFINTDs) is a step forward, offering mentorship to young scientists and helping them build expertise to mentor future generations. 21. Access to high-quality, peer-reviewed research has improved with open access policies and initiatives like BioMed Central's Open Access Africa, but significant investment is still needed to maintain access to electronic journals, databases, and other resources. 22. Limited internet access in disease-endemic countries further restricts researchers' ability to access open-access information, highlighting the need for better infrastructure and support for academic institutions. 23. Brazil's Federal Agency for the Support and Evaluation of Graduate Education (CAPES) provides a positive example by subscribing to major peer-reviewed journals, making scientific publications accessible to academic institutions across the country.
